idiom_name: private data member + one mediating member function (class-level guard); passkey token to narrow callers
implementation_notes: The classic proxy/real-subject pair collapses into the class's own access control: the resource is a private data member, every public member function is the check-then-delegate path, and the compiler enforces the single-entry property for ordinary code (access is checked whenever a member name is used, and 'if it does not satisfy the access rules, the program does not compile'). Where several collaborators may call one privileged operation, the passkey/attorney-client idiom - a token whose constructor is private to the intended friend - narrows the grant instead of a friend declaration that opens every private member. All of this is a language-level discipline, not a security boundary: the check is compile-time only, applies to names rather than objects, and a friend declaration, an explicit cast to a private base or code compiled into the same process can still reach the member. A protected system that must resist such code needs the OS variant (handle/descriptor ownership, separate process).
pitfalls: Access control is compile-time and name-based: a friend declaration, an explicit cast to a private base, pointer arithmetic or a macro defeats it - do not present private members as a security boundary against code you also compile.
This goes through a reference, pointer or span into the guarded state (or a const_iterator over it) hands the caller a path the guard no longer sees; return guarded views or copies.
friend is all-or-nothing and neither transitive nor inherited: prefer the passkey to avoid widening every private member for one operation.

Virtual dispatch has a trap: access is checked at the call site's static type and the final overrider's access is ignored, so a public base method can invoke a private override - 'private' gates names, not dispatch.
